title: How is bleeding severity assessed?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: How is bleeding severity assessed?
body.back: Where it is (external and internal), whether arterial or venous, and how much: losing over 25 percent of blood volume can cause shock. Check inside bulky clothing and under the patient.

title: How is external bleeding controlled?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: How is external bleeding controlled?
body.back: Check, Call, Care. Protect yourself; apply a dressing and press; pack deep wounds. A tourniquet for massive limb bleeding, as a last resort, ideally by a trained person.

title: How is a tourniquet applied?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: How is a tourniquet applied?
body.back: Wide flat non-stretch band 7.5 to 10 cm, wrapped several times just above the wound, overhand knot, stick on the knot, second knot, twist until bleeding stops, secure the stick, note the time. If over an hour from care, loosen slowly at 60 min with direct pressure; retighten if bleeding restarts.

title: How is a pelvic sling applied?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: How is a pelvic sling applied?
body.back: Empty pockets and remove the belt; slide the material under the buttocks, centre it on the greater trochanters, cross it over the front, tighten and secure with a knot, clamp or tape.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Assess severity. Where, arterial or venous, and whether more than 25% of blood volume is lost (shock).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Wound packing. Fill deep wounds with gauze to press on the bleeding source.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Direct pressure. Apply a dressing and press firmly: the first step.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Protect and call. Gloves, then call the EMS.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Pelvic sling. Centred on the greater trochanters, crossed in front and tightened.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Tourniquet. Last resort for life-threatening limb bleeding; note the time.

title: How do you assess bleeding severity?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: How do you assess bleeding severity?
body.back: Where it is (internal or external), arterial or venous, and whether more than 25% of blood volume is lost (shock risk).

title: What are the escalating steps to stop bleeding?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What are the escalating steps to stop bleeding?
body.back: Direct pressure with a dressing, then wound packing, then a tourniquet for massive limb bleeding.

title: Describe how to apply an improvised tourniquet.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Describe how to apply an improvised tourniquet.
body.back: Wide flat band 7.5 to 10 cm, wrapped close above the wound, overhand knot, stick, second knot, twist until bleeding stops, secure the stick, note the time.

title: What do you do with a tourniquet more than an hour from care?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What do you do with a tourniquet more than an hour from care?
body.back: Loosen very slowly at 60 min while pressing the wound; retighten if heavy bleeding returns; if controlled, leave it loose in place.

title: How is a pelvic sling applied?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: How is a pelvic sling applied?
body.back: Empty pockets and remove belts, slide the material under the buttocks, centre on the greater trochanters, cross over the front, pull tight and secure.

title: Define sudden cardiac arrest.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Define sudden cardiac arrest.
body.back: Sudden loss of organised cardiac activity with haemodynamic collapse, mostly from VF or pulseless VT, sometimes PEA or asystole. It needs immediate resuscitation, following the chain of survival.

title: Give the epidemiology and causes.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Give the epidemiology and causes.
body.back: 15 to 20 percent of deaths in industrialised nations, about half of cardiovascular deaths, and the first sign of heart disease in up to half. Elderly: coronary disease. Under 35: channelopathies, cardiomyopathies. Young athletes: HCM, anomalous coronaries. Non-cardiac: trauma, toxins, respiratory distress.

title: How do you recognise cardiac arrest?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: How do you recognise cardiac arrest?
body.back: Make sure it is safe; tap and shout; no response. Call 15. Open the airway and look for absent or abnormal breathing (agonal gasps, brief seizure-like activity); professionals check pulse for up to 10 s. If in doubt, start CPR.

title: Describe high-quality CPR.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Describe high-quality CPR.
body.back: Lower half of the sternum, 5 to 6 cm deep, 100 to 120/min, full recoil, no leaning, firm surface, minimal interruptions. 30 compressions to 2 breaths (mouth-to-mouth, mask or bag-valve-mask); continuous compressions if you cannot ventilate.

title: How is an AED used?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: How is an AED used?
body.back: Right pad below the right collarbone, left pad below the left armpit; pads must not touch; dry the chest; follow prompts. VF/pVT: shock then 2 min CPR. Asystole/PEA: 2 min CPR then reassess.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Defibrillator. Right pad below the right clavicle, left pad below the left armpit; follow the voice prompts.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Alert. Call the emergency services at once and get an AED.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Rescue breaths. 30:2 if trained; otherwise continuous compressions.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Chest compressions. Lower half of the sternum, 5 to 6 cm deep, 100 to 120 per minute, full recoil.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Recognise. Unresponsive with absent or abnormal (agonal) breathing: assume cardiac arrest.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Rhythm decision. Shockable (VF, pulseless VT) vs non-shockable (asystole, PEA), then 2 minutes of CPR.

title: Define sudden cardiac arrest.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Define sudden cardiac arrest.
body.back: Sudden cessation of organised cardiac activity with haemodynamic collapse, usually from VF or pulseless VT, sometimes PEA or asystole.

title: How do you recognise cardiac arrest?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: How do you recognise cardiac arrest?
body.back: Unresponsive to tap and shout, with absent or abnormal breathing (agonal gasps). In doubt, assume arrest and start CPR.

title: What are the features of high-quality compressions?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What are the features of high-quality compressions?
body.back: Lower half of the sternum, 5 to 6 cm, 100 to 120/min, full recoil, no leaning, minimal interruptions, firm surface.

title: Compression-to-ventilation ratio?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Compression-to-ventilation ratio?
body.back: 30:2 if trained; continuous compressions if unable or unwilling to ventilate.

title: Where do AED pads go?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Where do AED pads go?
body.back: Right pad below the right clavicle, above the nipple; left pad below the left armpit over the lower ribs. Not touching; dry chest.

title: Shockable vs non-shockable rhythms?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Shockable vs non-shockable rhythms?
body.back: Shockable: VF and pulseless VT, shock then 2 min CPR. Non-shockable: asystole and PEA, 2 min CPR then reassess.

title: Causes of sudden cardiac death by age?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Causes of sudden cardiac death by age?
body.back: Elderly: coronary artery disease. 35 and under: channelopathies and cardiomyopathies. Young athletes: hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, anomalous coronary origin. Non-cardiac: trauma, toxins, respiratory distress.

title: Define shock.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Define shock.
body.back: Widespread circulatory failure to oxygenate and nourish the body, disturbing mitochondrial energy transfer and producing toxic metabolites. Four types: distributive, hypovolaemic, cardiogenic, obstructive.

title: Describe the circulation.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Describe the circulation.
body.back: Macrocirculation generates oxygenated flow; microcirculation distributes it. Arteries are resistive, veins capacitive; exchange happens in capillaries. Perfusion depends on MAP, cardiac output and ventricular pressure.

title: Give the haemodynamic formulas.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Give the haemodynamic formulas.
body.back: MAP = CO x SVR = SV x HR x SVR. SV depends on preload, contractility and afterload. TaO2 = CaO2 x CO; CaO2 = 1.34 x Hb x SaO2. Fick: VO2 = CO x (CaO2 − CvO2). Hypoperfusion leads to anaerobic metabolism and lactic acidosis.

title: Describe the baroreflex.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Describe the baroreflex.
body.back: High arterial pressure increases carotid sinus firing, lowering sympathetic and raising parasympathetic activity, which lowers pressure; low pressure does the opposite.

title: Give the clinical signs of shock.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Give the clinical signs of shock.
body.back: Peripheral: mottling, cold, pale or cyanotic extremities, capillary refill over 3 s. Regional: altered consciousness, oliguria, tachypnoea, tachycardia.

title: How is shock assessed?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: How is shock assessed?
body.back: Non-invasive and invasive arterial pressure, central venous pressure, pulmonary artery catheter (Swan-Ganz), cardiac output by the Fick principle, echocardiography for stroke volume, arterial lactate and venous oxygen saturation.

title: Give the causes of each shock.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Give the causes of each shock.
body.back: Cardiogenic: infarction, myocarditis, drug toxicity, severe AV block, tachycardia, acute mitral or aortic insufficiency, thrombus, septal rupture. Hypovolaemic: haemorrhage, GI losses, burns, dehydration. Distributive: septic, anaphylactic, inflammatory, spinal. Obstructive: tamponade, pulmonary embolism, tension pneumothorax.

title: How is shock managed?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: How is shock managed?
body.back: Symptomatic: oxygen, vascular filling, catecholamines (adrenaline, noradrenaline, dobutamine: inotropy and vasoconstriction). Etiological: treat the cause specific to the type of shock.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Cardiogenic shock. Low contractility (MI, myocarditis), arrhythmias or mechanical causes.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Distributive shock. Sepsis, anaphylaxis, inflammatory states, spinal shock.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Hypovolaemic shock. Haemorrhage, GI losses, extensive burns, dehydration.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Arterial pressure. MAP = CO × SVR, with CO = SV × HR; SV depends on preload, contractility, afterload.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Obstructive shock. Tamponade, pulmonary embolism, tension pneumothorax.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Clinical signs. Mottling, cold extremities, capillary refill over 3 s, altered consciousness, oliguria, tachypnoea, tachycardia, high lactate.

title: Define shock.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Define shock.
body.back: Widespread failure of the circulation to oxygenate and nourish the body; alters mitochondrial energy transfer; a transition between life and death.

title: Key haemodynamic equations?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Key haemodynamic equations?
body.back: MAP = CO × SVR; CO = SV × HR; CaO2 = 1.34 × Hb × SaO2; TaO2 = CaO2 × CO; VO2 = CO × (CaO2 - CvO2).

title: Clinical signs of shock?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Clinical signs of shock?
body.back: Mottling, cold/pale/cyanotic extremities, CRT > 3 s; altered consciousness, oliguria, tachypnoea, tachycardia.

title: Causes of cardiogenic shock?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Causes of cardiogenic shock?
body.back: Reduced contractility (MI, myocarditis, intoxication), rhythm disorders (high-degree AV block, SVT), mechanical (acute MR or AR, thrombus, septal rupture).

title: Distributive shock: types and mechanism?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Distributive shock: types and mechanism?
body.back: Septic, anaphylactic, inflammatory (pancreatitis, burns), spinal; vasodilation and capillary leak cause relative hypovolaemia and poor O2 extraction.

title: How is shock assessed?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: How is shock assessed?
body.back: Arterial pressure (non-invasive/invasive), CVP, Swan-Ganz, cardiac output (Fick), echocardiography, blood gases with lactate and venous saturation.

title: Principles of shock management?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Principles of shock management?
body.back: Symptomatic: oxygen, fluids, catecholamines (adrenaline, noradrenaline, dobutamine). Etiological: treat the specific cause.

title: Describe the liver's blood supply.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Describe the liver's blood supply.
body.back: Liver: 2 lobes, 8 segments, about 1000 lobules. It receives 25 percent of cardiac output: the portal vein gives 75 percent of flow but 50 percent of oxygen; the hepatic artery gives 25 percent of flow and 50 percent of oxygen.

title: List the GI tract's functions.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: List the GI tract's functions.
body.back: Digestion, endocrine signalling, expulsion, protection (acid, immunity), motility, absorption, secretion and storage (stomach and colon). Thirst (osmoreceptors, baroreceptors) and hunger regulate intake.

title: List the liver's metabolic functions.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: List the liver's metabolic functions.
body.back: Glucose and glycogen; cholesterol and proteins; fat, protein and carbohydrate metabolism; drug metabolism by cytochrome P450; detoxification; bile; acute phase reactants; haemoglobin processing and iron storage; clotting factors; blood reservoir. Ammonia from deamination becomes urea.

title: How is liver function assessed?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: How is liver function assessed?
body.back: Damage: ALT, AST, AST/ALT, GLDH. Biliary: GGT, ALP, bilirubin. Synthesis: albumin, cholinesterase, prothrombin time. Only PT and albumin truly measure function.

title: Amylase versus lipase.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Amylase versus lipase.
body.back: Amylase: rises at 2 to 12 h, peaks at 24 h, normal in 3 to 5 days; not specific (salivary, renal, gynaecological, ischaemia) and may be normal in hypertriglyceridaemia. Lipase: rises at 4 to 8 h, peaks at 24 h, lasts 8 to 14 days; more sensitive and specific.

title: Which endoscopy and imaging are used?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Which endoscopy and imaging are used?
body.back: Upper endoscopy: dyspepsia, GERD with alarm signs, dysphagia, upper bleeding, anaemia, vomiting, ulcers, tumours, coeliac, Barrett's. Colonoscopy: lower bleeding, bowel change, IBD, radiological lesions. Ultrasound: liver lesions, gallstones. CT: obstruction, ischaemia, trauma. MRCP: bile duct stones. EUS: pancreatic cancer, strictures.

title: Describe drug-induced acute liver failure.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Describe drug-induced acute liver failure.
body.back: Commonest from paracetamol; also antibiotics, NSAIDs, antiepileptics, antituberculosis drugs, herbs. Mechanisms: toxic metabolites, immune attack on P450 adducts, apoptosis, mitochondrial failure (steatosis), bile duct damage (cholestasis). Brain oedema from ammonia and inflammation. Stop the drug, give N-acetylcysteine, consider transplant.

title: Describe acute mesenteric ischaemia.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Describe acute mesenteric ischaemia.
body.back: Sudden hypoperfusion of the small bowel and right colon from arterial or venous occlusion or non-occlusive causes. Pain out of proportion to exam, progressing to peritonitis and sepsis. CT angiography first. Restore flow (endovascular if no necrosis), resect necrotic bowel, preserve length.

title: Describe acute pancreatitis.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Describe acute pancreatitis.
body.back: Activation of digestive enzymes inside the pancreas causing autodigestion, which may spread to peritoneum and retroperitoneum and lead to SIRS and multi-organ failure. 80 percent from alcohol or gallstones (gallstones slightly more). Supportive care; ERCP for biliary obstruction.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Acute liver failure. Often drug-induced; paracetamol is the commonest cause.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Acute mesenteric ischaemia. Pain out of proportion to examination; CT angiography first.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Acute pancreatitis. 80% from gallstones or alcohol; autodigestion of the gland.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Pancreatic enzymes. Lipase rises in 4 to 8 h, stays up 8 to 14 days, and is more specific than amylase.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: True tests of liver function. Prothrombin time and albumin reflect synthetic function.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Hepatic blood supply. The liver gets 25% of cardiac output; the portal vein gives 75% of flow but 50% of oxygen.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Management. Supportive care, then NAC for paracetamol, revascularisation or resection, ERCP for biliary obstruction.

title: List the overall functions of the GI tract.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: List the overall functions of the GI tract.
body.back: Digestion, endocrine signalling, expulsion, protection, motility, absorption, secretion, storage; thirst and hunger regulate intake.

title: Describe the liver's blood supply.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Describe the liver's blood supply.
body.back: 25% of cardiac output; portal vein 75% of flow and 50% of O2; hepatic artery 25% of flow and 50% of O2.

title: Group the liver tests.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Group the liver tests.
body.back: Damage: ALT, AST, AST/ALT, GLDH. Biliary: GGT, ALP, bilirubin. Synthesis: albumin, cholinesterase, PT.

title: Amylase vs lipase in pancreatitis?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Amylase vs lipase in pancreatitis?
body.back: Amylase: rises 2-12 h, peaks 24 h, normal 3-5 days, non-specific. Lipase: rises 4-8 h, peaks 24 h, lasts 8-14 days, more sensitive and specific.

title: Mechanisms of drug-induced liver injury?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Mechanisms of drug-induced liver injury?
body.back: Toxic metabolites, immune attack on drug-P450 adducts, TNF-receptor apoptosis, mitochondrial dysfunction (ATP↓, ROS, steatosis), bile-duct damage (cholestasis).

title: Why does acute liver failure cause brain oedema?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Why does acute liver failure cause brain oedema?
body.back: Hyperammonaemia (glutamine accumulates in astrocytes), pro-inflammatory state, altered BBB, cerebral vasodilation.

title: Management of the three GI emergencies?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Management of the three GI emergencies?
body.back: Supportive care; NAC and transplantation for ALF; revascularisation or resection for mesenteric ischaemia; ERCP for biliary pancreatitis.

title: What does the endocrine system regulate?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What does the endocrine system regulate?
body.back: Sodium and water balance, blood volume and pressure; calcium and phosphate; energy and fuel use; responses to stress; reproduction, growth and ageing. Dysregulation affects many systems.

title: Describe the adrenal glands.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Describe the adrenal glands.
body.back: Cortex: glomerulosa (aldosterone), fasciculata (cortisol), reticularis (androgens, DHEA). Medulla: catecholamines and sympathetic activation. Central in the stress response.

title: Primary versus secondary adrenal insufficiency.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Primary versus secondary adrenal insufficiency.
body.back: Primary (Addison): gland destroyed, loses about 90 percent of function, no cortisol or aldosterone. Secondary: low ACTH, low cortisol; commonest after prolonged glucocorticoid use. Chronic causes: steroids, HIV, tuberculosis, autoimmune, congenital, infiltrative, cancer, surgery.

title: What precipitates adrenal crisis?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What precipitates adrenal crisis?
body.back: Drugs (steroid withdrawal, etomidate, ketoconazole), sepsis, adrenal or pituitary haemorrhage, Sheehan syndrome, trauma, liver failure, pancreatitis.

title: How does adrenal crisis present?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: How does adrenal crisis present?
body.back: Weakness, weight loss, anorexia, abdominal pain, fever; refractory hypotension that looks like septic shock; may mimic gastroenteritis; lack of reflex tachycardia. Labs: hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia; cortisol and ACTH vary with the cause.

title: How is adrenal crisis managed?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: How is adrenal crisis managed?
body.back: ABCs, saline bolus, rule out and treat sepsis, vasopressors as needed, send cortisol and ACTH, give hydrocortisone. Suspect it when hypotension resists vasopressors.

title: Compare insulin and glucagon.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Compare insulin and glucagon.
body.back: Beta cells: insulin increases glucose entry and glycogen, inhibits glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, lipolysis and fatty acid oxidation. Alpha cells: glucagon inhibits glycolysis, increases gluconeogenesis, glycogenolysis and beta-oxidation. Delta cells: somatostatin inhibits both.

title: Explain diabetic ketoacidosis.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Explain diabetic ketoacidosis.
body.back: No insulin: cells starve despite high glucose, fatty acids make ketones (acidosis); glycosuria causes osmotic diuresis and dehydration; acidosis shifts K+ out (serum high) while urine depletes K+ and bicarbonate. Presents with polyuria, polydipsia, abdominal pain, vomiting, confusion, Kussmaul breathing with fruity odour; critical: hypotension, coma. Treat with IV insulin, water and salt, electrolytes, monitoring; avoid hypokalaemia and cerebral oedema.

title: Explain thyroid storm.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Explain thyroid storm.
body.back: Extreme thyrotoxicosis (Graves', thyroiditis, tumours) triggered by infection, surgery, ACS, stroke, neck trauma, noncompliance, hormone ingestion or iodine contrast. HR over 140, fever over 41°C, sweating, GI and CNS symptoms; critical: high-output failure, AF, coma. Treat: ABCs, fluids, sedation, cooling, beta-blockade, PTU or methimazole, dexamethasone, iodine, treat the trigger.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Adrenal crisis. Acute severe adrenal insufficiency; classic sign refractory hypotension.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Diabetic ketoacidosis. Insulin lack: hyperglycaemia, ketones and acidosis.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Hypothalamus and pituitary. The hypothalamus leads the endocrine system through the anterior and posterior pituitary.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Adrenal crisis treatment. ABCs, saline, rule out sepsis, vasopressors, send cortisol and ACTH, give hydrocortisone.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: DKA treatment. IV insulin, water and salt, correct electrolytes, avoid hypokalaemia and cerebral oedema.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Thyroid storm treatment. Fluids, cooling, beta-blockade, PTU or methimazole, dexamethasone, iodine.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Thyroid storm. Life-threatening thyrotoxicosis with fever, tachycardia and CNS dysfunction.

title: List the key functions of the endocrine system.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: List the key functions of the endocrine system.
body.back: Sodium, water and blood pressure; calcium and phosphate; energy balance and fuel use; stress response; reproduction, growth and senescence.

title: Primary vs secondary adrenal insufficiency?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Primary vs secondary adrenal insufficiency?
body.back: Primary: adrenal destruction (Addison), cortisol and aldosterone lost. Secondary: low ACTH, often after prolonged glucocorticoid therapy.

title: Causes of chronic adrenal insufficiency?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Causes of chronic adrenal insufficiency?
body.back: Chronic steroids, HIV, TB, autoimmune adrenalitis, congenital (CAH, adrenoleukodystrophy), infiltration, cancer, surgery/irradiation, liver failure/pancreatitis.

title: Critical management of adrenal crisis?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Critical management of adrenal crisis?
body.back: ABCs, saline bolus, rule out sepsis, antibiotics if needed, vasopressors, send cortisol and ACTH, give hydrocortisone.

title: Actions of insulin vs glucagon?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Actions of insulin vs glucagon?
body.back: Insulin: glucose uptake, glycogen synthesis, inhibits glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, lipolysis, fatty-acid oxidation. Glucagon: the reverse, plus beta-oxidation.

title: Pathophysiology of DKA?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Pathophysiology of DKA?
body.back: Insulin lack → cell starvation → ketogenesis → acidosis; glycosuria → osmotic diuresis → dehydration; K+ shifts out (serum high) while total K is lost.

title: DKA treatment goals?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: DKA treatment goals?
body.back: IV insulin, replete water and salt, correct electrolytes, avoid hypokalaemia, reduce acidosis and ketosis, control glucose, prevent cerebral oedema.

title: Thyroid storm: presentation and treatment?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Thyroid storm: presentation and treatment?
body.back: HR > 140, fever > 41 °C, sweating, GI symptoms, delirium; fluids, cooling, beta-blockade, PTU/methimazole, dexamethasone, iodine, treat precipitant.

title: What does the immune system do?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What does the immune system do?
body.back: Recognises danger, tolerates self, eliminates threats and repairs tissues. Dysregulation causes immunodeficiency, hypersensitivity, autoimmunity or poor tumour surveillance.

title: Describe innate immunity.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Describe innate immunity.
body.back: First line: epithelial barriers and mucus; tissue macrophages, dendritic and mast cells that secrete cytokines; phagocytes (neutrophils, monocytes/macrophages); complement in blood. Two reactions: inflammation and antiviral defence (NK cells, type I interferons). Recognition by PRRs for PAMPs and DAMPs; it also stimulates adaptive immunity.

title: Describe adaptive immunity.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Describe adaptive immunity.
body.back: Needs antigen stimulation, proliferation and differentiation, taking several days. Humoral (B cells, antibodies) and cellular (T cells). Specific, with memory: secondary responses are faster and stronger.

title: How does immunity keep homeostasis?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: How does immunity keep homeostasis?
body.back: Macrophages clear dead cells silently with IL-10 and TGF-beta; dendritic cells induce self-tolerance without danger signals; NK cells kill cells lacking MHC I; complement C3b opsonises.

title: Primary versus secondary immunodeficiency.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Primary versus secondary immunodeficiency.
body.back: Primary: genetic, from birth; recurrent severe infections, growth delay, autoimmunity. IgA deficiency (commonest); SCID (no T and B cells, emergency transplant). Treated with immunoglobulins, marrow transplant, gene therapy. Secondary: acquired from HIV, chemotherapy, steroids, immunosuppressants, diabetes, organ failure, blood cancers; unusual infections and reactivations; treat the cause, vaccinate, cotrimoxazole prophylaxis in HIV.

title: Define hypersensitivity, allergy and atopy.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Define hypersensitivity, allergy and atopy.
body.back: Hypersensitivity: reproducible symptoms at a dose normal people tolerate. Allergy: hypersensitivity driven by immune mechanisms. Atopy: tendency to make IgE to low-dose allergens, with asthma or eczema. Type I: IgE, sensitisation then mast cell degranulation, histamine and leukotrienes: rhinitis, asthma, urticaria, anaphylaxis.

title: How is anaphylaxis recognised and treated?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: How is anaphylaxis recognised and treated?
body.back: Skin (urticaria, oedema), respiratory (bronchospasm, laryngeal oedema), GI, cardiovascular (hypotension, shock), loss of consciousness. IM adrenaline in the thigh without delay, supine with legs raised, oxygen, fluids, antihistamines, steroids, hospital monitoring.

title: Describe autoimmunity and tumour immunity.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Describe autoimmunity and tumour immunity.
body.back: Autoimmunity: loss of tolerance, autoantibodies or self-reactive T cells; SLE (anti-DNA), MS (T-cell demyelination); treated with immunosuppressants and biologics. Tumour surveillance: NK, CD8+, Th1, M1 macrophages. Escape: loss of MHC I, inhibitory molecules, suppressive cytokines, Tregs and M2 macrophages, T-cell exhaustion; basis of checkpoint antibodies and CAR-T.

title: Describe vaccination and transplantation.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Describe vaccination and transplantation.
body.back: Vaccines give safe antigen exposure to make memory B and T cells; boosters when immunity wanes or the pathogen changes (DTP, influenza). Rejection: hyperacute (preformed antibodies, thrombosis), acute (T cells, days to weeks), chronic (fibrosis, years). Immunosuppressants: steroids, calcineurin inhibitors, antiproliferatives, biologics; risks of infection, cancer and toxicity.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Adaptive immunity. Antigen-specific B and T lymphocytes; takes days; produces memory.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Cancer immunity. NK and CD8+ T cells kill tumour cells; tumours escape by losing MHC I and suppressing T cells.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Immunodeficiency. Primary (genetic: IgA deficiency, SCID) or secondary (HIV, drugs, chronic disease).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Transplantation. Hyperacute, acute and chronic rejection; immunosuppressants prevent it.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Immune homeostasis. Silent phagocytosis of dead cells, tolerance, NK killing of MHC I-negative cells.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Hyperactivity. Allergy (type I, IgE, mast cells) and autoimmune disease (SLE, MS).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Innate immunity. First line: epithelial barriers, phagocytes, complement, NK cells and type I interferons.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Vaccination. Safe exposure to antigen creates memory; boosters when immunity wanes or the pathogen changes.

title: What are the two main innate reactions?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What are the two main innate reactions?
body.back: Inflammation (leukocytes and plasma proteins against extracellular microbes and damaged tissue) and antiviral defence (NK cells, type I interferons).

title: Where does innate defence act?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Where does innate defence act?
body.back: Portals of entry (epithelia, mucus), tissues (macrophages, dendritic cells, mast cells), blood (complement).

title: How is immune homeostasis maintained?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: How is immune homeostasis maintained?
body.back: Silent phagocytosis with IL-10/TGF-β, dendritic-cell tolerance, NK killing of MHC I-negative cells, C3b opsonisation.

title: Primary vs secondary immunodeficiency?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Primary vs secondary immunodeficiency?
body.back: Primary: genetic, from birth (IgA deficiency, SCID). Secondary: acquired (HIV, chemotherapy, steroids, immunosuppressants, diabetes, organ failure, blood cancers).

title: Mechanism of type I hypersensitivity?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Mechanism of type I hypersensitivity?
body.back: Sensitisation produces IgE; re-exposure degranulates mast cells and basophils; histamine and leukotrienes cause vasodilation, bronchospasm, itch, oedema.

title: Mechanisms of tumour immune escape?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Mechanisms of tumour immune escape?
body.back: Loss of MHC I, inhibitory molecules, immunosuppressive cytokines, Tregs and M2 macrophages, T-cell anergy or exhaustion.

title: Three types of graft rejection?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Three types of graft rejection?
body.back: Hyperacute (minutes-hours, preformed antibodies), acute (days-weeks, T cells vs donor MHC), chronic (months-years, fibrosis).

title: Main immunosuppressants and risks?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Main immunosuppressants and risks?
body.back: Steroids, calcineurin inhibitors, antiproliferatives, anti-IL-2R/anti-CD3; risks: opportunistic infections, lymphomas and skin cancers, organ toxicity.

title: Explain the Monro-Kellie doctrine.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Explain the Monro-Kellie doctrine.
body.back: The skull is a fixed-volume box of brain, blood and CSF. Increasing any component raises ICP; lowering ICP requires reducing one of them, which is how every ICP treatment works.

title: Give normal ICP and perfusion.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Give normal ICP and perfusion.
body.back: ICP 5 to 15 mmHg, raised at 20 or more. CPP = MAP − ICP. The brain is 2 to 3 percent of body mass but takes 20 percent of blood volume. Autoregulation keeps flow constant for CPP 60 to 160 mmHg; below 60 ischaemia, above 160 hypertensive encephalopathy. PaO2 and PaCO2 also affect flow.

title: Describe the ICP waveform and vicious circle.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Describe the ICP waveform and vicious circle.
body.back: Baseline with small rapid cardiac pulsations and larger slower respiratory waves. Raised ICP lowers CPP, causing ischaemia, which causes more swelling and further raises ICP.

title: Name the types of cerebral oedema.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Name the types of cerebral oedema.
body.back: Vasogenic, cytotoxic, interstitial and osmotic; blood-brain barrier dysfunction is central. Hydrocephalus shows enlarged ventricles with effaced sulci.

title: Summarise ICP management.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Summarise ICP management.
body.back: Steroids for vasogenic (tumour) oedema; glucose control; hypothermia (lowers flow, ICP, metabolism); skull trephination for deteriorating epidural haematoma; craniotomy or ventriculostomy for space-occupying lesions; shunts for hydrocephalus.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Cerebral blood. Its volume rises with vasodilation, for example from high PaCO2.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Brain tissue. One of the three intracranial volumes; cerebral oedema enlarges it.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Cerebral perfusion pressure. CPP = MAP - ICP; autoregulated between 60 and 160 mmHg.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Cerebrospinal fluid. Accumulates in hydrocephalus; can be drained by ventriculostomy or shunt.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Monro-Kellie doctrine. Fixed-volume skull: more of one component means higher ICP unless another decreases.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Vicious circle. Low CPP causes ischaemia, which causes more swelling and higher ICP.

title: State the Monro-Kellie doctrine.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: State the Monro-Kellie doctrine.
body.back: The cranium is a fixed-volume space containing brain, blood and CSF; an increase in one raises ICP; lowering ICP means reducing one of them.

title: Normal and raised ICP values?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Normal and raised ICP values?
body.back: Normal 5 to 15 mmHg in adults; raised ICP is 20 mmHg or more.

title: What is CPP and its autoregulation range?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is CPP and its autoregulation range?
body.back: CPP = MAP - ICP; CBF is kept constant for CPP 60 to 160 mmHg; below 60 ischaemia, above 160 hypertensive encephalopathy.

title: Four types of cerebral oedema?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Four types of cerebral oedema?
body.back: Vasogenic (BBB breakdown, tumours), cytotoxic (cell swelling), interstitial (hydrocephalus), osmotic.

title: List the management options for raised ICP.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: List the management options for raised ICP.
body.back: Steroids (vasogenic oedema), glucose control, hypothermia, skull trephination (epidural haematoma), craniotomy or ventriculostomy, shunts for hydrocephalus.

title: Why is raised ICP a vicious circle?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Why is raised ICP a vicious circle?
body.back: Raised ICP lowers CPP, causing ischaemia, which causes more swelling and raises ICP further.

title: Define first aid and its aims.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Define first aid and its aims.
body.back: Immediate care for a sudden injury or illness before professional help: preserve life, prevent worsening, promote recovery. Used in medical emergencies, trauma, environmental and respiratory problems, poisoning and envenomation.

title: What is a first responder's role?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is a first responder's role?
body.back: Anyone trained or not: stay calm, act within your knowledge, call professionals, and secure the scene before acting.

title: How do you secure the scene?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: How do you secure the scene?
body.back: Look over the setting, hazards and victims before rushing in; remove dangers; do not assume severity; protect yourself from blood and fluids with PPE. At a road crash: ignitions off, casualties to safety, immobilise upright vehicles, never right one on its side.

title: Describe the three Cs and ABCDE.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Describe the three Cs and ABCDE.
body.back: Check the victim with a primary survey (Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability including neck injury, Exposure), Call EMS (15 in Morocco) with an exact location, Care for the victim.

title: How do you manage an unresponsive breathing victim?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: How do you manage an unresponsive breathing victim?
body.back: Check breathing for up to 10 s; open the airway (head tilt-chin lift, or jaw thrust if trauma); clear blood, vomit and dentures with a finger sweep; place in the recovery position (left side if pregnant); keep checking breathing.

title: How do you manage choking?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: How do you manage choking?
body.back: Partial: encourage coughing. Complete (no speech, cough or air): remove visible objects, 2 to 4 back blows, then Heimlich (fist below the ribs, 2 to 3 sharp squeezes). Small child: face down. Infant: 5 back blows then 5 chest thrusts. Obese or pregnant: chest thrusts. Untreated, it leads to hypoxic cardiac arrest.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Open the airway. Head tilt with chin lift, or jaw thrust if trauma is suspected.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Call the emergency services. Dial 15 in Morocco and give the exact location.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Primary survey. ABCDE to find life threats first.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Choking. Back blows between the shoulder blades, then abdominal thrusts.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Recovery position. On the side, so vomit or blood drains; left side in pregnancy.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Secure the scene. Look before rushing in, remove dangers, protect yourself with PPE.

title: What are the three aims of first aid?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What are the three aims of first aid?
body.back: Preserve life, prevent the condition from worsening, promote recovery.

title: What is the first responder's role?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is the first responder's role?
body.back: Stay calm, act within your knowledge and training, call for professional help, and secure the scene before acting.

title: List ten scene hazards.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: List ten scene hazards.
body.back: Biohazards/chemicals, fire and fumes, electricity, water, traffic, falling objects/unstable structures, slippery surfaces, sharp edges/glass, explosives, confined spaces, heights, aggressive people.

title: What do you do at a road accident scene?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What do you do at a road accident scene?
body.back: Switch off all ignitions, move casualties to safety, immobilise an upright vehicle (hand brake, wheel blocks), never right a vehicle on its side, stabilise it only if safe and trained.

title: What is the primary survey?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is the primary survey?
body.back: The first examination to find life threats, using ABCDE: Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure/Environment.

title: How do you check breathing?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: How do you check breathing?
body.back: Look, listen and feel for normal breathing for at most 10 s; listen for wheeze or stridor; look for swelling, choking, cyanosis; pulse oximetry if available.

title: How do you clear the airway of debris?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: How do you clear the airway of debris?
body.back: Sweep the mouth with two fingers to remove blood, vomit, loose dentures and debris, without pushing objects deeper.

title: Partial vs complete airway obstruction?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Partial vs complete airway obstruction?
body.back: Partial: can speak or cough forcefully, so encourage coughing. Complete: no speech, no air exchange, no cough, hands at the neck; leads to hypoxic cardiac arrest.

title: Describe the Heimlich manoeuvre.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Describe the Heimlich manoeuvre.
body.back: From behind, arms around the victim, fist in the upper abdomen just below the ribs, 2 to 3 sudden firm squeezes to force out the object.

title: What do the kidneys do?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What do the kidneys do?
body.back: Filtration, reabsorption, secretion and excretion; fluid, electrolyte and blood pressure regulation; hormones: erythropoietin, active vitamin D and renin.

title: Describe renal blood flow and GFR.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Describe renal blood flow and GFR.
body.back: RBF 20 percent of cardiac output. The glomerulus lies between afferent and efferent arterioles. GFR = Pnet x area; glomerular hydraulic pressure about 60 mmHg. Normal 120 (women) to 130 (men) mL/min/1.73 m², about 180 L/day, falling 1 mL/min/year after 40; estimated by creatinine clearance.

title: Describe autoregulation and the JGA.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Describe autoregulation and the JGA.
body.back: Flow and GFR stay stable for perfusion 80 to 180 mmHg. Lower perfusion lowers NaCl delivery to the macula densa (NKCC2), signalling granular cells to release renin, also released by sympathetic tone.

title: How is water reabsorbed?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: How is water reabsorbed?
body.back: Passively in the proximal tubule, loop and distal tubule along osmotic gradients, then ADH-dependent in the collecting duct, reducing urine to about 1 percent of filtrate.

title: Describe prerenal AKI.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Describe prerenal AKI.
body.back: The commonest (40 to 55 percent): hypoperfusion from true hypovolaemia (haemorrhage, GI or renal losses, third spacing) or low effective arterial volume (cardiogenic or septic shock, cirrhosis, hypoalbuminaemia, anaphylaxis). Parenchyma intact; reverses with perfusion; prolonged, it causes ATN.

title: Describe intrinsic AKI.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Describe intrinsic AKI.
body.back: Tubulointerstitial: ischaemic and septic ATN (commonest), allergic interstitial nephritis, nephrotoxic drugs (aminoglycosides, amphotericin, cyclosporine, tacrolimus, ACE inhibitors, NSAIDs, contrast), endogenous toxins (haemoglobin, myoglobin, bilirubin, uric acid in tumour lysis). Vascular: renal artery thrombosis or embolism, atheroembolism, HUS, malignant hypertension, rejection, vasculitis, scleroderma.

title: Describe postrenal AKI.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Describe postrenal AKI.
body.back: Obstruction of both ureters (or one with a solitary kidney), bladder outlet or urethra: stones, clots, papillae, compression. Commonest: bladder neck (prostate, anticholinergics, neurogenic bladder). Relief restores GFR if obstruction was short.

title: How does AKI present?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: How does AKI present?
body.back: Early often silent; later vomiting, diarrhoea, thirst, cramps, oedema, flank pain, less urine. Hypovolaemia: tachycardia, hypotension, dry mucosa, sunken eyes. Hypervolaemia: oedema, weight gain, oliguria. Also confusion, fever, uremic encephalopathy (asterixis, stupor), livedo (atheroembolism), rash (allergy).

title: How is AKI managed?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: How is AKI managed?
body.back: Correct reversible causes, avoid further injury, keep fluids and electrolytes normal, nutrition and glycaemic control; no drug treats AKI itself. Prerenal: fluids. Postrenal: catheter, nephrostomy or stent. Intrinsic: stop culprit drugs, immunosuppression for glomerulonephritis. Diuretics only for overload. Dialysis for refractory overload, uremic pericarditis, severe electrolyte or acid-base disorders. Prevent by avoiding nephrotoxins and maintaining perfusion.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Complications. Pulmonary oedema, hyperkalaemia, hypocalcaemia, hyperphosphataemia, acidosis, uraemia.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Normal GFR. About 120 (women) to 130 (men) mL/min/1.73 m², about 180 L/day.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Intrinsic AKI. Ischaemic or septic ATN, interstitial nephritis, nephrotoxins, vascular disease.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Juxtaglomerular apparatus. Low NaCl at the macula densa or low perfusion triggers renin release.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Postrenal AKI. Bilateral ureteric, bladder outlet or urethral obstruction.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Prerenal AKI. The commonest (40 to 55%): true hypovolaemia or low effective arterial volume; reversible.

title: List the renal functions.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: List the renal functions.
body.back: Filtration, reabsorption, secretion, excretion; homeostasis and blood pressure regulation; erythropoietin, vitamin D activation, renin.

title: How does the JGA regulate GFR?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: How does the JGA regulate GFR?
body.back: Low perfusion or low NaCl delivery to the macula densa (NKCC2) signals granular cells to release renin; autoregulation between 80 and 180 mmHg.

title: Prerenal AKI: causes?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Prerenal AKI: causes?
body.back: True hypovolaemia (haemorrhage, GI/renal losses, third spacing) or low effective volume (cardiogenic/septic shock, cirrhosis, hypoalbuminaemia, anaphylaxis).

title: Intrinsic AKI: causes?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Intrinsic AKI: causes?
body.back: ATN (ischaemic, septic), allergic interstitial nephritis, nephrotoxins, endogenous toxins (Hb, myoglobin, urate), large- and small-vessel disease.

title: Postrenal AKI: causes?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Postrenal AKI: causes?
body.back: Bilateral ureteric obstruction (or unilateral with solitary kidney), bladder outlet (prostate, anticholinergics, neurogenic bladder), urethral obstruction.

title: AKI management by type?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: AKI management by type?
body.back: Prerenal: fluids. Postrenal: catheter, nephrostomy or stent. Intrinsic: stop culprit drugs, immunosuppression for GN or vasculitis.

title: Immediate complications of AKI?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Immediate complications of AKI?
body.back: Pulmonary oedema, hyperkalaemia, hypocalcaemia, hyperphosphataemia, metabolic acidosis, uraemic seizures, coma, bleeding, encephalopathy.

title: Describe the trauma primary survey.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Describe the trauma primary survey.
body.back: Airway with cervical spine stabilisation, Breathing, Circulation with control of external haemorrhage, Disability (neurological status), Exposure with hypothermia prevention.

title: How is circulation assessed in trauma?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: How is circulation assessed in trauma?
body.back: Peripheral and central pulses and skin colour. Palpable pulse approximates minimum systolic BP: radial 80, femoral 70, carotid 60 mmHg. Major haemorrhage sites: chest, abdomen, retroperitoneum, thigh, external.

title: How is the cervical spine protected?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: How is the cervical spine protected?
body.back: Suspect injury after falls, dives, crushes, road or sports accidents. Minimise neck movement; let alert patients hold their neck; never force. Unresponsive supine: kneel behind and use head or trapezius squeeze; improvised collars, extrication splints, spine boards with padding.

title: Give the splinting rules.
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Give the splinting rules.
body.back: Remove clothing, check neurovascular status before and after, cover open wounds with sterile dressing, immobilise the joints above and below, cool and elevate, reassess.

title: How is a motorcycle helmet removed?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: How is a motorcycle helmet removed?
body.back: Two rescuers: one holds in-line stabilisation with fingers on the mandible; the other cuts the strap, takes over stabilisation from below (mandible and occiput); the first spreads the helmet sideways over the ears, tilting it to clear the nose, removing glasses first. Contraindicated if neck pain or impaled object.

title: How is an amputated part preserved?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: How is an amputated part preserved?
body.back: Control bleeding first; wrap the part in a moist sterile dressing, place in a watertight bag, then in a second bag of ice or ice-water; never freeze.

title: How are burns managed?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: How are burns managed?
body.back: Stop burning: remove from source, roll or wrap to extinguish, remove hot clothing and jewellery. Chemical: water for at least 10 min, no neutraliser; hydrofluoric acid: then calcium gluconate gel; phosphorus: keep covered with water. Eyes: copious irrigation. Primary survey, then cool water 1 to 5°C for about 30 min; longer cooling of large areas risks hypothermia.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Primary survey. Airway with C-spine, Breathing, Circulation with haemorrhage control, Disability, Exposure without hypothermia.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Amputated part. Wrapped in moist dressing, bagged, then placed in ice water, never frozen.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Burns. Stop the burning process, remove jewellery, cool with water for about 30 minutes.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Helmet removal. One rescuer holds in-line, the other removes the helmet, spreading it over the ears.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Spinal motion restriction. Manual in-line stabilisation of the head and neck when a spinal injury is suspected.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Splinting. Immobilise the joint above and below; check neurovascular status before and after.

title: What is the trauma primary survey?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: What is the trauma primary survey?
body.back: Airway with C-spine stabilisation, Breathing, Circulation with haemorrhage control, Disability, Exposure while preventing hypothermia.

title: Minimum systolic pressure by palpable pulse?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: Minimum systolic pressure by palpable pulse?
body.back: Radial about 80, femoral about 70, carotid about 60 mmHg.

title: When do you suspect a cervical spine injury?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: When do you suspect a cervical spine injury?
body.back: Falls or dives from height, crushing by machinery or heavy objects, road traffic and sporting accidents.

title: General splinting guidelines?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: General splinting guidelines?
body.back: Expose the limb, check neurovascular status before and after, dry sterile dressing on open wounds, immobilise joint above and below, cool and elevate, reassess.

title: How do two rescuers remove a motorcycle helmet?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: How do two rescuers remove a motorcycle helmet?
body.back: R1 holds in-line from above; R2 cuts the strap and takes over (mandible angle and occiput); R1 spreads it over the ears, removes glasses, tilts it back over the nose; R1 then holds the head again.

title: How do you preserve an amputated part?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: How do you preserve an amputated part?
body.back: Control bleeding first; wrap in moist clean cloth, seal in a bag, place in a second bag of ice or ice water; cold, never frozen.

title: How do you stop the burning process?
subject: subj:firstaid

body.front: How do you stop the burning process?
body.back: Remove the source, roll or wrap a burning victim, remove hot clothing and jewellery; rinse chemicals with water at least 10 min, no neutraliser.
